title: The King's Role in a Crisis: A Conversation with Lord Young
label: 16 September 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: The Constitution Committee heard from Lord Young of Old Windsor, former principal private secretary to the sovereign, about the monarch's constitutional role. He described the weekly audience between the sovereign and the Prime Minister, the importance of confidentiality, and the reserve powers that the monarch holds but rarely uses. Lord Young argued that the system relies on good faith and that the sovereign acts as a last-resort arbiter, but that the constitution's flexibility and the good behaviour of politicians has so far prevented any serious crisis.

chapters.title: The Weekly Audience
chapters.takeaway: The private weekly meeting between the monarch and the Prime Minister is central to the constitution, allowing frank discussion and advice.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Young, welcome. You spent nearly 20 years working for the Royal Household. How would you describe the monarch's constitutional role today?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Thank you. I was in the room for the appointment of six or seven Prime Ministers. The core of it was the weekly audience—usually on a Wednesday after PMQs. The Prime Minister would come to Buckingham Palace, sometimes with a debrief afterwards.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: The private secretary would see the PM alone first, then the PM would have an hour with the Queen. Meanwhile, I'd spend that hour with the PM's principal private secretary—the 'golden triangle'—to make sure there was never a gap between Head of State and Head of Government.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: And the privacy of that meeting?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Absolutely crucial. Without it, the PM couldn't speak candidly. The Freedom of Information Act protects the formulation of policy, and the same principle applies here. If these conversations were public, the whole system wouldn't work.

chapters.title: Reserve Powers and Good Faith
chapters.takeaway: The monarch has reserve powers for extreme situations, but they rely on good faith and the fear of their use is often enough to prevent crisis.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Could the monarch ever act as a restraint on a Government beyond that weekly hour?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, in theory. The sovereign has the right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn. But if a PM says 'Thanks, but I'll do it my way', that's the compact. Reserve powers might come into play if it's unclear who should be PM, or if a PM asks for a dissolution when they've clearly lost confidence.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: But when things work well, it never gets to that. The fear that the sovereign might say no is itself a restraint. I call it the 'good faith' theory—not 'good chap', which is a bit dated. It depends on people acting responsibly.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is that opacity helpful for novel situations?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I think so. Because our constitution is unwritten, it can evolve. During Covid, when Boris Johnson was seriously ill, we had to work out what to do if a PM was incommunicado. There was no precedent. We worked it out on a call—the Cabinet Secretary would summon the Cabinet and they'd decide on a temporary PM. It never happened, but it showed the system can adapt.

chapters.title: Guardians and Transparency
chapters.takeaway: The private secretary to the monarch is one of many constitutional guardians, and trust is built through long-term, non-partisan service rather than transparency.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Who guards the constitution? Is the private secretary a guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: Yes, among many others. The principles have been consistent since the 1950s. My predecessor Alan Lascelles wrote a letter to The Times in 1950 setting out principles—that was a form of guardianship. These days, anonymous letters might not work, but the role still involves anticipating problems.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about transparency and trust? The public wants to know what's going on.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: There's a paradox: how do you have trust without transparency? The monarchy's advantage is its long-term perspective. It's not about tomorrow's headlines. By consistently acting in the national interest, over years, trust is built. It's about visibility and service, not just secrecy.

chapters.title: Extreme Scenarios and Safeguards
chapters.takeaway: In extreme scenarios, such as a Government censoring the press or refusing to resign, the monarch's power is limited by democratic legitimacy and practical politics.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What if a Government elected on a manifesto commitment introduced censorship? Could the monarch intervene?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: If it was a manifesto commitment and passed by Parliament, it would be very difficult for the sovereign to overturn that. In a democracy, the monarch can't simply interfere with the democratic process.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What about a PM who loses a vote of no confidence but refuses to resign?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: In practice, that PM would quickly lose their Cabinet and be unable to govern. The system would crumble around them. The sovereign has reserve powers, but they're a last resort. The 1975 Australian dismissal is often cited, but the situation there was different—supply was blocked. Most experts think it's unlikely today.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So are our constitutional safeguards sufficient?

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Old Windsor
turns.text: I wouldn't say complacent, but I can't see a better system. That doesn't mean we shouldn't be vigilant. I'd like to see the Cabinet Manual updated regularly—it's stuck in 2011. That would give me more comfort.
